news.title: Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out
news.source_text:
Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out
A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.
In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.
OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.
However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.
Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.
A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.
So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.
You can try it yourself here.
What the Model Does
Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:
- Open: no schema supplied. The model reads the page and works out which parts of it are structured fields (a label followed by a value, a table with a header row over its columns) from context and layout, not from a fixed list of field names, and returns everything it finds as key-value pairs.

news.summary: Hugging Face has released the Dharma Field Extractor, a 2-billion‑parameter model that extracts specified fields from any document type and returns them as structured JSON, outperforming larger LLMs at lower cost. The model supports open schema extraction or exact schema requests, making it suitable for high‑volume invoice processing, medical requisition parsing, and contract data extraction.
news.enterprise_use: Go to your document ingestion pipeline and integrate the Dharma Field Extractor API to replace costly OCR + manual mapping workflows this week. Failing to adopt it risks higher processing costs and slower data onboarding, potentially delaying downstream systems like Freshservice ticketing or JumpCloud provisioning. The most affected tool is your OCR/ETL layer, which can now directly output JSON ready for Google Workspace or Azure AD data imports.

news.title: Introducing Images 2.6
news.summary_raw: Images 2.6 brings faster image generation, GIF creation, more precise editing, and new API controls across ChatGPT, Codex, and the API.
news.source_text:
We’re introducing Images 2.6 in ChatGPT, Codex, and the API, bringing your ideas to life faster. With this, you can bring motion to your images with GIFs — from animating a brand mascot or character to turning a product shot into an eye-catching loop. You can also create polished visuals faster and refine them with greater precision — keeping characters, products, and brand details consistent as you edit.
People around the world now create 4 billion images per week across ChatGPT, Codex, and the API. On average, that’s more than half a billion images created per day.
Images 2.6 generates images 50% faster than before. In the API, we offer GPT‑Image‑2.6 Flare and Sunburst for developers to choose from. When quality is set to low, Flare can generate images in as little as six seconds. For work that calls for greater detail and precision, GPT‑Image‑2.6 Sunburst brings higher-quality image generation and even greater image consistency across edits when quality is set to medium or high. Flare also improves layout quality for posters, product imagery, and other professional visuals.
For moments that call for motion, GIFs bring another dimension to your ideas. Marketers and creators can animate a brand mascot for a campaign, create reactions and memes for social media, or use animated storyboards to explore character movement before video production.
And you don’t need a polished design to get started — even a simple sketch can become an expressive, animated character for videos, games, and more.
From personal reactions to brand mascots and product visuals, GIFs give people and businesses a playful way to communicate. Town, a startup building an AI work assistant, used Images 2.6 in the API to explore how animated characters could bring more personality to everyday interactions at work.
With Images 2.6, developers get more control over how images are created, edited, and carried into the next stage of a project. Image markup, already available in ChatGPT, comes to the API so teams can pinpoint exactly where to make specific changes. SVG exports make designs ready to use across websites, apps, and print.
A new complexity parameter lets developers adjust how much planning the model does to meet a request, with lower settings suited to quick edits. Image quality controls visual detail and fidelity, while complexity guides how much goes into the scene.
For most editing tasks, we recommend low complexity for faster edits, paired with the image quality your workflow requires. For scenes with many elements or constraints, try medium or high complexity effort.

news.title: A YC startup is putting $1M behind five unsolved materials science problems for AI
news.summary_raw: Discovered Materials, a months-old YC startup that uses AI to find chip materials, is offering $200,000 for each solution to five open materials science problems.
news.source_text:
Discovered Materials, a months-old, San Francisco startup using AI models to find new substances for building advanced chips, announced a million-dollar challenge for AI models to solve five critical problems in materials science.
While frontier AI models have solved a remarkable series of outstanding mathematics problems and made progress in the life sciences, they have yet to truly plumb the complex physics in advanced materials.
“It’s more difficult to specify problems clearly in materials science because it’s not like math, where you have a very specific definition and can get to a yes or no,” said Advaith Sridhar, a co-founder of Discovered Materials, which was part of Y Combinator’s spring 2026 batch. “We came to this discussion [wondering], what are the grand challenges in this field? How do we know AI is making progress?”
Though materials science doesn’t have an equivalent of the Millennium Prize Problems, Discovered Materials recruited an advisory group of academics at leading global universities to spell out five open problems. The company is offering a pool of prizes, worth $1 million in total, for solutions to the problems.
- A theory to explain cuprate superconductivity, or the ability of certain materials to have zero electrical resistance at ultra-low temperatures.
- A numerical method to predict the structures of interfaces between silicon and silicon dioxide, a material combination found in almost all semiconductors.
- A numerical method to map grain structure to thermal properties, enabling the design of better heat dissipation materials.
- A theory to predict why shining light on materials can change their behavior, particularly around superconductivity.
- A numerical method to improve Density Functional Theory, a key technique used in materials science to model the structures of atoms and molecules.
“Across materials science, there are phenomena we observe but cannot explain,” Felipe Jornada, a Stanford professor who helped develop the challenges, said in a statement. “Explaining these phenomena would improve our understanding of physics, and the answers would directly shape how we build electronics, store energy, and manufacture the materials of the future.”
Before announcing the challenges, Discovered Materials turned frontier lab models loose on them, giving AI agents internet access and other resources to work autonomously for days. The models spent several days on each problem without making much headway. Still, it’s easy to imagine OpenAI or Anthropic attempting to one-shot them with significantly more compute or a newer model.
“It’s not particularly a concern to us whether we find it, or someone else finds it, or a professor finds it, or the frontier labs find it,” Sridhar said. “The reason we’re putting out these challenges is because we want them to serve as the goalposts. If you go and solve these challenges, we are deepening our understanding of materials and how things around us behave.”

news.title: Agility is the first pure humanoid robot company on the stock market. Are you buying?
news.summary_raw: Agility arrives on the Nasdaq today as the first publicly-traded pure-play humanoid robotics company.
news.source_text:
Almost a year ago to the day, Figure AI CEO Brett Adcock responded to some gentle social media taunting from rival robotics company Agility with a prediction: “You’ll be bankrupt in <12 months.”
Instead, Agility is going public through a reverse-merger that will see it become a publicly-traded company and raise $465 million in new capital from retail investors and a tranche of private funding. The transaction will take place through a special purpose acquisition company, or SPAC.
“You don’t see a lot of dancing robots or backflipping robots from Agility,” CEO Peggy Johnson told TechCrunch ahead of the company’s market debut. “We stuck to our strategy, which [are] these manual, very repetitive jobs, that it’s hard to find humans to do.”
Agility predates the recent boom in physical AI investment. The company was spun out of Oregon State University in 2015 by a group of researchers who made headway in figuring out how to get a robot to walk safely on two legs. The company has focused on deploying a handful of its Digit robots in industrial settings with nine different customers, including Schaeffler, GXO, Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada, and Mercado Libre. Digits are generally used to move heavy totes, including more than 100,000 of them at a GXO logistics facility.
Compared to humanoid robots built by Figure, Tesla, 1X, or Boston Dynamics, Agility’s Digit can seem plodding, but the robot is actually doing real work, and earning money — albeit just $174,000 in the first six months of 2026, and mostly from related parties. The company lost $362 million in the same time period, which means the clock is ticking for it to successfully deploy its infusion of new capital.
The good news is that Agility has $300 million in planned contracts from 30 customers for its new generation of robot, Digit 5. The new model can safely operate around humans, not just in an isolated work cell like its previous model (and indeed most humanoid robots). That deal was “one of the driving factors” behind the decision to take the company public, Johnson said, but could not yet reveal who the customers or say if they are investors.
To close the deals, Johnson said that Digit 5 will have to hit undisclosed targets along several metrics, including throughput, uptime, and accuracy of placement. The company has yet to show off the prototypes of Digit 5, but Johnson said they will be demonstrated at CES 2027 and widely available at the end of that year.
The company’s pitch is that a robot can save $100,000 a year for companies under a robot-as-a-service model and even more if the customer purchases the robot outright. Whether those unit economics work out in the end will depend on Digit 5’s capabilities, both in terms of task accuracy, and how long it can work without pauses for recharging or maintenance.

news.summary: Agility, a pure humanoid robotics company, has gone public via a SPAC, raising $465 million to develop its next-generation Digit 5 robot. The new model promises safer human interaction and higher throughput, aiming to secure $300 million in contracts by end‑2027.

news.title: Finding New Drugs Is Laborious. This AI Startup Is Skipping The Lab Work
news.summary_raw: Potential Sciences, a startup backed by the UK government, is betting that training AI models on computer-generated biochemical data can speed up the plodding process of developing new drugs.
news.source_text:
A new British startup believes that artificial intelligence is the key to speedrunning the slow and temperamental process of drug design.
Potential Sciences plans to build large-scale chemical datasets by using basic principles of physics to simulate interactions between atoms, then small molecules, then complex amino acids and proteins. With that data, it’s betting it can train AI models and prediction systems capable of identifying highly targeted drugs for specific diseases, bypassing costly and time-consuming lab experimentation.
“We want molecules that are never going to work in the clinic to fail fast,” Hatem Helal, Potential Science’s founder and CEO, tells WIRED. “That means having better predictors of how they will behave as they interact with human biology.”
The startup, which launched on November 5, says it has seed funding in the tens of millions of dollars from SovAI—the UK government’s AI venture capital fund—and Twin Path Ventures, among other investors. The founders declined to disclose the precise figure or valuation.
If things pan out as Potential Sciences hopes, it could pave the way for the accelerated development of new treatments for all sorts of diseases. By reducing the cost of experimentation, Helal says, the company’s approach could also make it economical for pharmaceutical companies to pursue drugs for rare conditions that have previously gone untreated.
“We want to make it possible to have more bespoke treatments for diseases—this idea that medicines can be one-off molecular combinations that are tailored to your unique human biology,” he says.
The question is whether Potential Sciences will be able to predict how well drug candidates will bind to disease-related proteins as accurately as it hopes, which would require a marked leap forward.
“I’m sure it will be an improvement,” says Peter Wolynes, a professor of chemistry at Rice University. But currently, “the engineering is at the level of the Romans, not of the Renaissance, in terms of how protein engineering is done,” he says.
Industry luminaries like Demis Hassabis, who won the Nobel Prize for Chemistry for his work at Google DeepMind, have long said that advances in AI will eventually lead to momentous scientific breakthroughs, in the same way the technology has recently carved up mathematics. The hope among startups like Potential Sciences is that drug discovery will be one of the first scientific frontiers to be transformed by the technology.
At the moment, a large proportion of AI drug discovery labs are developing models on top of a single public database of 3D atomic structures—the Protein Data Bank—which researchers have expanded over decades with the results of new experiments. The problem, according to Helal, is that the dataset remains too small to train AI models advanced enough to reliably accelerate the search for viable drug candidates.

news.summary: Potential Sciences, a British AI startup, is using physics-based simulations to generate large chemical datasets for training AI models that predict drug efficacy, potentially accelerating drug discovery without lab work. The company launched on November 5 with seed funding from SovAI and Twin Path Ventures and aims to enable bespoke treatments for rare diseases.

news.title: AI’s Next Trick? Speaking Dolphin
news.summary_raw: Denise Herzing, the founder and director of the Wild Dolphin Project, is using AI to help understand audio and video footage of the marine mammals.
news.source_text:
Large language models are already communicating with humans in dozens of languages everyday. Turns out it may not be a stretch to use them to talk with dolphins, too.
That’s the premise of research by Denise Herzing, the founder and director of the Wild Dolphin Project. Herzing first began thinking about how the marine mammals communicate while on a 1985 trip to the Bahamas to study Atlantic spotted dolphins after hearing their telltale clicks and whistles.
It’s been a 40-year wait, but AI is finally allowing Herzing to untangle what dolphins are saying, she told the audience at WIRED World Fair. Her research group has gathered countless hours of video and audio footage of dolphins, and it’s now working with scientists at Georgia Tech as well as Google DeepMind to give structure to dolphins’ language—if not fully translate it yet.
“With AI, we can find patterns,” she said, adding, “This is a powerful new tool. I’ve personally been waiting for it.”
The team has used some of that research to even attempt two-way communication by rigging up an underwater, wearable computer that can play dolphin sounds. That includes using sounds to indicate items like a scarf and habitat like sargassum—a seaweed. Two researchers would model behavior—one researcher would play the scarf sound, for instance, and then the other would play with it—and then see how the dolphins responded.
One of the challenges, though, is decoding communication from mimicry. “Even though we had these whistles and are labeling toys, there’s a big difference between mimicking and understanding the function,” Herzig said. “That’s hard to do in the wild.”
Working in a sanctuary or more controlled environment might help researchers suss out the difference, she said.
What dolphins are actually saying to each other remains a bit of a mystery. While Herzig’s team has done a job of finding patterns, a two-way conversation remains a ways off. That’s because while humans have made pretty decent headway in understanding dolphin social hierarchies and behavior, there’s more work needed to really enable a conversation.
“We might have the data and the structure, but what does it mean in dolphin culture?” she said. “That’s going to be an exploration on its own.”
Being able to talk with dolphins would, of course, be very cool. (Who hasn’t dreamed of talking with animals after all?) But ultimately our attempts to understand dolphins could help us understand more about ourselves and our relationship with the planet. Herzig said that when she asks people what they think dolphins would say to us, the most common response is along the lines of “the dolphins would say ‘Why are you messing up our ocean?’”
That answer, she said, “tells you how we are thinking about the world.”
news.summary: A research team led by Denise Herzing has teamed up with Google DeepMind to decode dolphin vocalizations using large language models, aiming toward two‑way communication with marine mammals. The work demonstrates AI’s expanding capability to model complex, non‑human communication systems, though it remains far from practical application.

news.title: Awesome repositories are no longer awesome
news.summary_raw:
Article URL: https://erikgahner.github.io/posts/2026/awesome-repositories-are-no-longer-awesome/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50377821
Points: 114
# Comments: 57
news.source_text:
Awesome repositories are no longer awesome
On GitHub, you will find a lot of repositories with the prefix 'awesome'. They usually contain curated knowledge and resources related to a certain domain, such as awesome-python (see, e.g., this repository for a list of awesome repositories). I used to see these awesome repositories as potential goldmines of good content. However, nowadays I see most of them as irrelevant and useless. There are two reasons for this, and they are both related to AI.
First, as many of these awesome lists get older, they contain a lot of outdated material if they are not actively maintained. You are in most cases better off simply asking a decent AI model for inspiration or the material you need. That is, I find it difficult to believe that most of these awesome lists are of interest to people anymore. If they remain useful, it will mostly be for agents looking to find and check relevant resources.
I had a quick look at the awesome-R repository. The repository was last updated more than a year ago, and most of the resources included in the overview are either outdated or will not be of general interest to people using R. One of the first links in the repository is an overview of the top 50 downloaded packages - as of 2016! This is simply not a good resource if you want to explore R in any shape or form.
Second, a lot of these awesome repositories are being flooded with AI slop. Go to any random awesome repository these days and you will most likely find a lot of pull requests suggesting the most generic tools and resources. For example, take a look at this awesome-free-online-tools repository. It is a small, unknown repository with 13 stars but 91 open pull requests at the time of writing. I did not look at all of these pull requests, but the ones I looked at all suggested generic vibe-coded tools.
I found this resource because of a pull request made to one of my repositories, a simple project where I store material I like related to statistics. The suggestion was to add StatOrigin ("a free, open database of industry statistics"), and once I had a quick look at the resource and the other pull requests made by the user, I could easily close the PR. This user alone has created at least six vibe-coded websites (StatOrigin, ScanChess, Sticker Printer Hub, QuizQuip, LiquidityPools, DefiLPKit) and submitted more than 100 pull requests to various awesome lists to add these websites.
It did not take me long to find examples where these tools were merged into the relevant repositories (see, e.g., here, here, and here). However, I also found examples where people did the basic work of checking out the material, such as here, where the PR was closed with the following explanation: "There is not yet sufficient evidence of qualified educator review, independent validation of the educational content, or demonstrated learning outcomes." Good stuff!
My point is not that these awesome repositories are now all bad. They can still be awesome
news.summary: The article argues that many GitHub 'awesome' lists have become outdated or cluttered with generic AI‑generated content, making them less useful for developers seeking reliable resources. It highlights that relying on AI models for inspiration may be more efficient than sifting through these stale repositories.
news.enterprise_use: Check your internal code‑base or documentation repositories for similar 'awesome' lists that may have accumulated outdated or low‑quality contributions; consider pruning or replacing them with curated, AI‑generated references to keep resources current.

news.summary:
The post traces the history of password hashing in Unix and SSH, explaining how the '*' placeholder in /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow evolved to prevent login and how crypt() handling of NULL and failure states changed over time.
It highlights the security implications of legacy authentication mechanisms and the importance of correctly handling crypt() failures in modern systems.
news.enterprise_use:
Check that your SSH and PAM configurations properly reject accounts with '*' or NULL hashes and ensure your local libc (musl, glibc) is up-to-date to avoid legacy bugs that could lead to authentication bypass.
Missing this check could allow attackers to craft inputs that exploit mis‑handled hash failures, potentially causing denial‑of‑service or unintended authentication.
Your JumpCloud or SSO integration should enforce that all user accounts in your directory have valid, non‑placeholder passwords and that the underlying OS rejects any attempt to authenticate with a '*' hash.

news.title: Dropbox acquires Tigris Data for $350M to bolster its AI infrastructure
news.summary_raw: The deal is expected to support the development of DBX Agent Cloud, a new storage platform aimed at developers building AI models and agents.
news.source_text:
Dropbox is making a big push into AI infrastructure with a $350 million acquisition of cloud technology company Tigris Data, marking what appears to be its largest acquisition to date.
Announced Thursday, the deal is expected to strengthen Dropbox’s AI infrastructure capabilities and support the development of DBX Agent Cloud, a new storage platform aimed at businesses and developers building AI models and agents.
Dropbox told TechCrunch via email that the transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026. The company also said it currently has no plans to reduce headcount as part of the acquisition. The company already cut 9% of its global workforce last month, WSJ reported.
DBX Agent Cloud will initially offer object storage as a stand-alone product, allowing businesses to purchase storage independently and use it with existing tools and applications built for Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service), which is a cloud storage service that enables businesses to store and retrieve large volumes of data.
Beyond its infrastructure ambitions, Dropbox is also bringing more AI capabilities to its core product. Users will be able to ask AI to perform supported tasks using their files, choose between different AI models, and connect their Dropbox content to third-party tools, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Muse.
The company also plans to expand DBX Agent Cloud with additional capabilities designed to help AI systems work with different types of content, including documents, images, audio, and video. Other planned additions include filesystem features that will allow AI agents to manage files and maintain continuity across tasks and sessions.
Dropbox says the updated experience has already reached more than 70,000 teams. The initial rollout is available to eligible Standard and Advanced customers in the U.S., U.K., and Australia, with broader availability planned for 2027.
Tigris Data was founded by former Uber engineers who helped develop the ride-hailing company’s storage infrastructure. The company provides cloud storage technology that helps businesses store and access data across different regions. Its platform automatically positions data closer to the users and computing resources that need it, helping reduce access times and improve performance.
Tigris Data raised $25 million in a Series A funding round last year.
While the Tigris deal appears to be Dropbox’s largest acquisition, it is not the company’s first move to expand its AI capabilities through M&A. Dropbox has previously acquired several AI-focused companies, including Reclaim.ai, Promoted.ai, and Mobius Labs.
news.summary: Dropbox has acquired Tigris Data for $350M to expand its AI infrastructure, enabling the upcoming DBX Agent Cloud platform that offers AI-friendly storage for models and agents. news.title: Alpine Linux Security advisory: OpenSSH-server password authentication bypass

Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50379704

news.source_text:
Security advisory: openssh-server password authentication bypass
If you run sshd on Alpine Linux, update openssh now and restart sshd.
Upgrading the package alone does not replace the running daemon.
If you cannot update yet, at least disable password logins: set
PasswordAuthentication no in your sshd configuration and restart sshd.
Either one closes the hole.
What is the problem?
An attacker who can reach your SSH port can log in without knowing any password. It takes one connection, works every time, and needs no retries.
The attacker needs the name of an account whose password field is *
(an account with no password set, which is normal for key-only accounts), and
needs the machine to have at least one other account with a $5$ or $6$
password hash. The attacker then sends a very long password (257 to 1024
bytes). One user with a password is enough: it makes every account without
one reachable.
Details are in the OpenSSH 10.6p2 release notes. No CVE identifier had been assigned at the time of writing.
Who is affected?
You are affected if all of the following are true:
- You run the Alpine openssh-serverpackage, which is built without PAM, or you runopenssh-server-pamwithUsePAM no. (openssh-server-pamwithUsePAM yesis not affected.)
- PasswordAuthenticationis- yes(the OpenSSH default, unless you changed it).
- The machine has an account whose password field is *. This includes:- root, which ships as- root:*in the base image since about Alpine 3.16. OpenSSH’s default- PermitRootLogin prohibit-passwordprotects root, so root is only reachable if- PermitRootLogin yesis set. That does not help if another account that can log in is able to become root, for example through- doas.
- Any key-only user created with adduserwithout a password, or withusermod -p '*'.
- Users coming from a directory service through musl-nscd (nslcd, winbind, sssd), since they have no shadow entry.
- The alpineuser in the official tiny-cloud images (see below).
 
- At least one local account has a $5$or$6$password hash.
Affected releases: every Alpine release we checked, 3.21 through 3.24 and edge, and the older releases that no longer receive regular updates (3.16 to 3.20).
Who is not affected?
- Docker and other container users that do not run sshdin the container.
- Systems with PasswordAuthentication no.
- Systems using openssh-server-pamwithUsePAM yes(withUsePAM noyou are affected).
- Locked accounts: those with !as the password field in/etc/shadow(a line startinguser:!:). They cannot log in with a password or a key.
- Systems where no account has a $-style password hash.
- Cloud images configured through cloud-init, which writes
PasswordAuthentication no.

apk upgrade -U -a

news.title: Exclusive: Aina’s Smart Ring Wants to Be a Remote Control for Your AI Agent
news.summary_raw: The startup Aina bets you won’t need to rely on your phone to control virtual assistants. It’s making a smart ring that lets you control the actions of your autonomous agents with one tap.
news.source_text:
Apoorv Shankar believes that in the very near future, humans will interact with technology through a series of approvals and rejections. AI agents will proactively come to us to complete tasks, and humans will say, “Yes, order that Uber,” or “No, don't get lunch from that spot.”
But if you get multiple pings from an AI agent throughout the day, taking out your phone to say yes or no every single time will be a “bottleneck,” he says. That's why he made the Aina Ring. It has a small display and a joystick-like button that lets you quickly accept or reject an AI agent's actions with your hands. Your phone can stay in your pocket.
Aina has been in stealth for the last 15 months, though the company debuted a few experimental products at CES 2026 under a different name: Project Mirage. One was called Dune—think of it as the precursor to the Aina Ring. Connect it to your Mac and the three buttons become context-aware controls based on what you're doing. In a meeting? The buttons can turn into shortcuts for mute, camera off, or record.
Aina studied how people used Dune and developed the Aina Ring, which it’s announcing today. Preorders are live now, and the ring costs $399 for a limited time before the retail price rises to $499 when it starts shipping in January 2027.
“Approvals are going to be the future of interfaces and interaction, and we wanted to build a device that just made it easy to approve stuff,” Shankar says.
This isn't Shankar's first time with a smart ring—he previously was the vice president of hardware at Ultrahuman, a fitness- and health-tracking ring that competed with Oura. (Ultrahuman was briefly banned in the US after a patent dispute with Oura.)
The team explored other gadgets like smart glasses and pendants, but ultimately decided the ring was the most convenient way to interact with agents. The titanium Aina Ring connects to Macs or iPhones, and at any moment, the onboard assistant is looking for the three things you need next. It learns your routines from your personal data, like location, calendar, and email, and after you connect various third-party services in the Aina app, like Uber or Spotify.
If you usually go for a run at 6 am, as soon as you put on your running shoes, it will suggest continuing the podcast you started last night, or play music—the ring's joystick doubles as a music-playback controller. If it's 8:30 am and you usually take an Uber to work, it'll suggest the ride—flick yes on the ring, and it'll handle the task right away. If you're running late for a Zoom meeting, Aina will ask if you want the assistant to send an email saying you'll be late. Shankar calls these “Aina Cues,” powered by the ring's Context Aware Operating System.
Many of these actions will likely be limited based on what apps and features are supported, though Shankar says users can create their own Cues using natural language. So if you want the ring to prompt you about turning on the coffee machine every morning at 8 am, you can configur
news.summary: Aina has launched a smart ring designed to serve as a hands‑on remote control for AI agents, enabling users to accept or reject tasks via a joystick and small display. The device connects to Macs and iPhones, leveraging personal data and third‑party services to provide context‑aware prompts and actions throughout the day.

news.title: He Trolls AI Labs for a Living. Now They All Want to Work With Him
news.summary_raw: OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceXSI have all reached out to Husk, an influencer who regularly goes viral by exposing the shortcomings of chatbots.
news.source_text:
OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI have all asked creator Matt Husk to collaborate following the viral success of his videos trolling AI models.
During the WIRED World Fair on Wednesday, Husk told the crowd “all the big AI companies” have inquired about working with him, including Elon Musk’s xAI, which Husk claimed offered a Tesla for a week if he made videos exclusively for the firm.
The comedian has gained some 2 million followers combined across Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube, as well as a deal with the talent agency Unicorn, through videoing himself making deadpan requests to ChatGPT’s voice model—asking it to count to 100, or to beatbox, for example. His viral videos have exposed the weaknesses of OpenAI’s LLM, which comically botches the tasks and swings between sycophancy and gaslighting Husk, and earned him the title of “Sam Altman’s worst nightmare.”
In April, Altman, nodding and smiling, admitted on tech podcast Mostly Human that the model’s inability to set an accurate timer was a “known issue” and would be for another year, after being shown a Husk video in which he asked ChatGPT to time him running a mile and found that it measured a span of a few seconds as lasting “around 10 minutes.” When Husk says “I swear I was faster than that,” it replies with a sympathetic tone: “It can feel faster in the moment.”
During his interview at WIRED World Fair with Shell Game podcast host Evan Ratliff, Husk said OpenAI offered him early access to a patch for the timer issue if he shared his account. He declined. The company had previously emailed Husk asking to collaborate on a video. “They offered me the smallest amount,” he said. “I was just like, ‘No.’” The firm then offered to send him gifts and asked for his home address; Again, Husk declined.
OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI (which was recently rolled into SpaceX to create SpaceXAI and then SpaceXSI after President Trump renamed artificial intelligence “super intelligence”) did not respond to requests for comment.
AI labs are increasingly pitching their products as capable of handling everyday chores. On Tuesday, OpenAI announced its model had scored “very highly” on a benchmark built to model its ability to help people in their personal lives, such as meal prep and enrolling a child in kindergarten. “The way they promote it is like ‘It can do anything,’” Husk said, “so I’ll put it to the test—see if it can order bread for me.” In one of his videos, Husk asks AI to help him negotiate some bread on Craigslist down from a starting price of $10,000 to $5. The model accepts a price of $400.
Husk began publicly trolling chatbots about a year ago. He told Ratliff, a WIRED contributor, at the time he liked to make TikToks asking people questions, but there weren’t many around while he was working his landscaping job, and he ran out of ideas. So he recorded himself telling ChatGPT a nuclear bomb had gone off. The model’s response, “I’m rooting for you,” and advice to take shelter “was not helpful at all,” he said
news.summary: Matt Husk, a viral AI critic, has attracted offers from OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI after exposing flaws in their language models. While the story highlights model limitations, it does not directly impact the IT engineer’s current stack.
news.enterprise_use: Keep an eye on OpenAI’s upcoming patch updates for model reliability—review their release notes over the next 30 days to gauge any improvements that could affect internal automation tools.

news.title: Detecting signs of hypertension using wearable sensors
news.source_text:
November 5, 2026
Paolo Di Achille, Staff Research Scientist, and Ming-Zher Poh, Senior Staff Research Scientist, Google Research
We present a new AI system that leverages standard consumer smartwatch sensors to passively detect signs of high blood pressure.
Hypertension (i.e., high blood pressure), often called the "silent killer”, affects over one billion people globally, yet more than half of adults with the condition are unaware they have it. Because it rarely presents with obvious symptoms, high blood pressure (BP) is typically discovered only through incidental screening. This gap in awareness is particularly severe among younger adults aged 18 to 44, where missing diagnoses can delay life-saving early interventions and significantly increase the long-term risk of adverse cardiovascular events like stroke or heart failure.
Office BP measurement serves as the primary initial screening gateway for detecting hypertension. In recent years, cuffless wearable devices have emerged as a potential tool to complement episodic office care. However, existing commercial solutions usually require regular calibration using a traditional arm cuff. This means they only track relative changes from a baseline cuff reading rather than identifying absolute hypertensive states, limiting their utility as independent screening tools.
In a new study published in Nature, we present a multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) system capable of passively detecting signs of hypertension using a consumer smartwatch, without requiring any cuff calibration. Dubbed AI-PPG-ACC-HTN, we validated this system against the clinical gold standard of 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM), and it achieves accuracy levels comparable to traditional cuff-based diagnostic workflows for both initial and confirmatory screening. These research findings helped inform the blood pressure trends Health Guardian feature in the Google Health app.
Instead of attempting to estimate exact, point-in-time systolic and diastolic blood pressure values, which are highly susceptible to transient environmental noise, our system reframes the problem. It focuses on identifying an individual’s underlying, persistent hypertensive state by aggregating passive physiological signatures over multiple days.

This allowed the model to discover complex, physiologically rich features of vascular and mechanical cardiac function without requiring manual feature engineering or medical labels.

news.title: Aina’s smart ring has a screen, a joystick and a mic so you can talk to AI agents
news.summary_raw: Aina's ring can also take calls and help you dictate notes on your Mac.
news.source_text:
Hardware startup Aina released a smart ring today that features a screen, a joystick, and a mic so that you can talk to your agents and take notes. The $399 ring has a speaker so you can take calls using it as well.
The startup, which raised $5.5 million in July, is positioning the ring as a controller of sorts for both AI and non-AI apps.
The company previously made Mirage, a three-key controller that let you invoke buttons based on the app on your Mac’s screen. For instance, if you were on a Google Meet call, you could map keys to camera on/off, mic mute/unmute, or to leave the meeting.
Aina has baked in lessons from that device to create the new ring, which it’s simply calling “AI ring.” Using its mic, you can take notes, send a prompt to agents, set reminders, and dictate notes on your Mac using Wispr Flow or the startup’s own dictation engine.
Now, there are already smart rings in the market that do similar things, like the Pebble Index 01, Sandbar Stream, Oasis, and Natura, which is probably why Aina has added more controls and functionality to stand out. Its ring comes with a speaker so that you can take calls, and there is a screen, which lets you see notifications from your phone or which apps you are controlling.
For navigation, there is a joystick, and it also supports gestures, so that it can trigger different actions based on what’s on your Mac or phone’s screen. The ring also lets you control music or even smart home devices like Apple TV.
I have used the ring for a few days, and it feels like a smartwatch in a ring format with more controls. I can get notifications and reply to them. It surfaces my meetings; I can call Uber if I want to get a ride home.
It’s easier to use Apple TV’s remote itself, but the Aina ring proved useful the couple times I couldn’t find the remote. Granted, a lot of the software and features are still being fleshed out, so it’s hard to figure out where such a device ring might sit in my daily usage, but it is squarely aimed at folks who are surrounded by digital devices and AI applications.
“Phones and laptop screens were designed for an age of browsing where you think about opening apps. For interacting with proactive agents, we need a better interface, and that is what we had in mind while designing Aina,” Apoorv Shankar, Aina’s founder, told TechCrunch over a call.
Companies are trying to cater to programmers and AI enthusiasts with specialized hardware that could help them harness different agents. This includes OpenAI’s experimental keyboard and Rabbit trying to position itself as a controller. The hope with such hardware is that enough people will have multiple agents running to invest in specific gadgets to keep tabs on them.
Aina’s ring goes on pre-order starting Thursday at early-bird pricing of $399, and the company plans to start shipping the device in January 2027. Once the early-bird period ends, the ring will cost $499.
news.summary: Aina has announced a new smart ring that includes a screen, joystick, microphone, and speaker, enabling users to interact with AI agents and control various apps directly from the ring. The device positions itself as a versatile controller for both AI and non‑AI applications, aiming to enhance productivity for tech‑savvy users.
news.enterprise_use: Check the Aina ring’s compatibility with your organization’s endpoint security policies and ensure it does not bypass existing device management controls. If your team uses Google Workspace or other cloud services, evaluate whether the ring’s AI interactions could expose sensitive data or create new attack vectors. Update your MDM and access management rules to account for any new device types.

news.title: Reddit Founder Says Building Social Media Apps Is ‘Not Cool Anymore’
news.summary_raw: Alexis Ohanian is trying to figure out what’s next for user-generated content now that so much of the internet is “compromised.”
news.source_text:
Alexis Ohanian wants to figure out the future of user-generated content. According to the Reddit cofounder, building social media apps is “not cool anymore” and so much of the internet has been compromised.
“I'm expecting some better version of the group chat to be that new version of UGC,” Ohanian told WIRED senior correspondent Lauren Goode at the inaugural WIRED World Fair.
Ohanian has a complicated relationship with the internet. He resigned from Reddit in 2020, following the killing of George Floyd, to make room for a Black board member and to pressure the company to reform its content moderation policies. The social site had been notorious for hosting violent and harmful rhetoric. Ohanian reflects on recently learning someone with a Reddit tattoo—once a sign of the site’s success to Ohanian—had since covered it up: “I don’t blame him.”
He now runs venture capital firm Seven Seven Six, which has over $1.3 billion in assets under management. He focuses on sports, where he finds real-life communities “in the age of AI slop” and a “manipulated” internet.
Ohanian is a proponent of the “Dead Internet Theory”—the idea that a lot of online activity and content is being generated by bots. Large language models have turbocharged this, with AI agents outrunning human users. “The internet that I grew up on … that was really built for humans first; user interfaces and experiences are going to go away,” said Ohanian, “because more of the internet is going to get created for these agents to use, [rather] than for people.”
In some ways, the advance in generative AI has been lucrative for sites like Reddit, which has licensed its vast archive of human conversations to companies including Google and OpenAI to train AI models. “Platforms like ours became very, very valuable to LLMs,” Ohanian said.
But the technology has also undermined the business. Reddit shares plunged 29 percent last week after the platform warned that Google’s AI-powered search was hurting referral traffic. Ohanian also worries the commercialisation of these conversations means they are full of “bullshit.” “The internet has gotten so manipulated because it is so incredibly valuable to do so,” he said.
Reddit recently said it would require users to sign in to fight third-party scraping and keep up user engagement. While Ohanian declined to say whether he agrees with the move, “there has to be provable humanity on the internet without being creepy.”
An early Anthropic investor, Ohanian is nonetheless optimistic about the potential benefits of AI. He is especially excited to see medical breakthroughs from the technology. “There is still a very real chance that this technology can cause a lot of harm for sure,” he said. “I think we have to be sober about how we're building and what we're doing, but I still can't help but see all of the things that can get so demonstrably better.”
news.summary: Reddit cofounder Alexis Ohanian has expressed concerns that user-generated content platforms are becoming obsolete as AI agents dominate online interactions. He warns that the rise of generative AI is both creating value for data-driven companies and eroding traditional internet business models, citing Reddit's recent share drop and policy shifts to combat scraping.

news.title: Axiom Math wants to keep AI slop out of mathematics
news.summary_raw: As AI floods math with unchecked proofs, Axiom Math is betting on verification. The startup’s AI agents just formally verified the Stacks Project, one of the field’s biggest libraries.
news.source_text:
It feels like AI is cracking a new math problem every week. Last month, OpenAI alone released 719 manuscripts claiming solutions to some of the field’s hardest problems. Even the computer checks can slip. After years of AI slop, it’s fair to wonder whether math is next.
AxiomMath is betting math can avoid that fate, not by slowing down, but by standing on firmer ground. The $1.6B startup wants to build a verified foundation that AI agents can rely on to write software and, eventually, do science.
On Wednesday, the company announced it had formally verified the Stacks Project, one of the largest bodies of mathematics ever written by humans. Mathematicians often hold Stacks in rare regard—Columbia mathematician Peter Woit has claimed there’s “nothing else really comparable,” comparing the project to “the famous Bourbaki books,” a series that rebuilt math from its foundations in the 20th century.
Woit’s Columbia colleague Johan de Jong started the Stacks Project in 2005 as an open-source reference. Mathematicians have contributed to it ever since, building out results from college-level algebra all the way up to the field’s most advanced ideas across algebra, geometry, and number theory.
The company’s fleet of AI agents translates the library’s roughly 7,654 pages into about 16 million lines of computer-checked code.
Formalizing math is a way of making sure the structure underneath it is sound. Mathematicians rewrite the proof as code in a programming language called Lean, and a program called a proof assistant checks the code line by line. If the proof passes, mathematicians can trust that it’s logically sound.
Engineers use the same idea, called formal verification, to confirm their chip designs work, while researchers in France have used it to catch bugs in software that calculates family benefits.
For a library like the Stacks Project, checking each theorem is only part of the job. The theorems and definitions in Stacks are interconnected, and each one builds on the ones before it. Like a family tree, many results in Stacks trace back to the ones that came before it.
That interconnectedness made Axiom unsure the project would work at first. The team had to keep every connection intact across about 16 million lines of Lean code.
“Things that are big and things that are delicate in life just don’t go together,” Axiom CEO Carina Hong told TechCrunch. “[Stacks] is a collection of mathematical results that is the foundation of mathematics. You want [theorems] to be consistent and not, like, paradoxical. You want the definitions to not fight with each other.”
The 25-year-old CEO dropped out of a Stanford math Ph.D. program nd founded the company in March 2025. In March, Axiom raised a $200 million Series A led by Menlo Ventures.
“We were not sure if vibe coding would be able to preserve the beauty of Stacks,” Hong said.

news.summary: Axiom Math has formally verified the Stacks Project, a massive open-source mathematics library, using Lean proof assistants to translate and validate 16 million lines of code. This milestone showcases a new AI-enabled approach to ensuring mathematical correctness that could influence formal verification practices in engineering.
